subject: Biology
title: Why Cells Divide
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why Cells Divide usable.

hook.text: Your body makes about 3.8 million new cells every second to replace those that die.

buildup.text: Cells divide for growth, repair, and reproduction. Without division, wounds never heal.

discovery.text: As a cell grows, its surface can't keep up with its volume. It must split or starve.

twist.text: Some cells like neurons rarely divide after birth. Gut lining cells divide daily.

climax.text: Division is tightly controlled. Checkpoints ensure DNA is copied correctly before splitting.

punchline.text: Divide or die. Most cells choose divide.

quiz.question: Why must cells divide as they grow larger?
options: Surface area can't keep up with volume

details.summary: Cells divide for three essential reasons: growth of the organism, repair of damaged or worn-out tissues, and reproduction. Division is tightly regulated by internal checkpoints and external growth signals to ensure it occurs only when needed and with accurate DNA copying.
details.whyItMatters: Cell division is the basis of all growth and tissue maintenance. When regulation fails, uncontrolled division leads to cancer. Understanding why and when cells divide is fundamental to developmental biology, medicine, and cancer research.
takeaways: Cells divide for growth, tissue repair, and organismal reproduction
Division is controlled by checkpoints that verify DNA integrity
Growth factors and contact inhibition regulate when division occurs

faq.question: What stops cells from dividing endlessly?
faq.answer: Multiple mechanisms: cell cycle checkpoints verify DNA integrity at each stage, contact inhibition stops division when cells touch neighbors, telomere shortening limits the number of divisions, and growth factor removal signals cells to stop dividing.

faq.question: Why do some cells divide faster than others?
faq.answer: Cells in high-turnover tissues like skin, gut lining, and bone marrow divide frequently because they face constant wear. Cells in stable tissues like liver divide rarely. Neurons and cardiac muscle cells almost never divide in adults.
